interactions.label: Which mechanism best explains why combined use of tobacco and alcohol increases

params.question: Which mechanism best explains why combined use of tobacco and alcohol increases oral and oesophageal cancer risk multiplicatively?

answers.text: Alcohol enhances mucosal permeability to tobacco carcinogens and generates acetaldehyde, a direct carcinogen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Alcohol amplifies carcinogen penetration through the mucosa and independently generates acetaldehyde, a direct carcinogen. This dual action drives field cancerisation — genetic damage across wide mucosal areas before any visible lesion appears.

answers.text: Alcohol causes direct thermal injury to the mucosa, creating entry points for tobacco carcinogens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Alcohol does not cause thermal injury. It acts as a solvent that increases mucosal permeability to carcinogens and independently generates acetaldehyde through its own metabolism.

answers.text: Tobacco and alcohol independently target the same proto-oncogene, doubling the mutation rate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Tobacco and alcohol act through different molecular mechanisms — tobacco delivers polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines, while alcohol generates acetaldehyde and enhances carcinogen absorption across the mucosa.

answers.text: Alcohol suppresses local T-cell immunity, allowing tobacco-damaged cells to escape immune surveillance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While alcohol affects systemic immunity, its primary carcinogenic role in the oral and oesophageal mucosa is enhancing carcinogen permeability and generating acetaldehyde through metabolism.

overallFeedback.feedback: Alcohol amplifies tobacco carcinogen penetration through the mucosa and generates acetaldehyde, a direct carcinogen. This synergy drives field cancerisation — wide areas of genetic damage well before any visible lesion appears.

Excellent. Alcohol's dual role — enhancing carcinogen absorption and generating acetaldehyde — explains the multiplicative risk with tobacco and the phenomenon of field cancerisation across the oral and oesophageal mucosa.

interactions.label: A gastric biopsy reveals individual tumour cells with abundant intracytoplasmic

params.question: A gastric biopsy reveals individual tumour cells with abundant intracytoplasmic mucin infiltrating the stomach wall diffusely without forming glands. Which molecular alteration most likely drives this pattern?

answers.text: APC tumour-suppressor gene loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. APC loss initiates the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in the colon (Vogelstein model), not diffuse gastric carcinoma. APC is the gatekeeper gene for colonic neoplasia.

answers.text: KRAS oncogene activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KRAS activation drives growth of established colonic adenomas, promoting villous architecture. It does not underlie diffuse-type gastric carcinoma.

answers.text: Loss of E-cadherin due to CDH1 gene mutation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Loss of E-cadherin — the cell-adhesion protein encoded by CDH1 — allows individual tumour cells to infiltrate without forming glands, producing signet-ring cells and the rigid leather-bottle stomach of linitis plastica.

answers.text: Helicobacter pylori CagA-induced chronic atrophic gastritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. H. pylori-driven atrophic gastritis initiates Correa's cascade leading to the intestinal type of gastric carcinoma, which forms discrete glands — the opposite of the diffuse pattern described here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Diffuse-type gastric carcinoma is driven by loss of E-cadherin (CDH1 gene), not by Correa's cascade. Without cell adhesion, individual tumour cells infiltrate diffusely, forming signet-ring cells and producing linitis plastica — the rigid leather-bottle stomach.

Well done. CDH1 loss abolishes E-cadherin-mediated cell adhesion, producing the characteristic diffuse infiltration, signet-ring cells, and linitis plastica — fundamentally distinct from the intestinal type that follows Correa's cascade.

params.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with chronic ileocaecal disease. Biopsy shows well-formed granulomas. Which combination of features most reliably indicates intestinal tuberculosis rather than Crohn disease?

answers.text: Small, scattered, non-caseating granulomas with longitudinal fissure ulcers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Small, scattered, non-caseating granulomas with longitudinal fissures are hallmarks of Crohn disease. Tuberculosis produces large, confluent granulomas with caseation.

answers.text: Non-caseating granulomas with fistula formation and skip lesions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fistulae and skip lesions are hallmarks of Crohn disease. Tuberculosis rarely causes fistulae and typically produces a hyperplastic stricturing mass.

answers.text: Crypt abscesses with continuous mucosal inflammation extending from the rectum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Crypt abscesses and continuous mucosal inflammation spreading from the rectum upward describe ulcerative colitis, not tuberculosis or Crohn disease.

answers.text: Large, confluent, caseating granulomas with transverse ulcers encircling the bowel

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Intestinal TB produces large, confluent, caseating granulomas and transverse girdle ulcers that encircle the bowel. This distinction is critical — giving steroids for undiagnosed TB can trigger disseminated disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Intestinal TB shows large, confluent, caseating granulomas with transverse girdle ulcers. Crohn disease shows small, non-caseating, scattered granulomas with longitudinal fissures and fistulae. Always exclude TB with an IGRA or biopsy PCR before starting steroids.

Excellent. Caseating, confluent granulomas with transverse ulcers reliably point to intestinal TB — a distinction that must be made before starting immunosuppressive therapy for presumed Crohn disease.

params.question: A patient presents with dysphagia that has progressed from solids to liquids over several months. Endoscopy reveals an annular, infiltrative oesophageal lesion. Why does oesophageal carcinoma typically present at an advanced stage?

answers.text: The oesophageal epithelium regenerates rapidly, masking early tumour growth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Rapid epithelial regeneration does not mask tumour growth. The key anatomical factor is the absent serosa, which allows silent circumferential spread through the wall.

answers.text: The oesophagus lacks a serosal layer, allowing tumour to spread circumferentially through the wall without early symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The oesophagus is unique among GI organs in lacking a serosa. Without this barrier, carcinoma infiltrates circumferentially through the wall, encircling the lumen before causing significant obstruction — hence the progression from solid to liquid dysphagia.

answers.text: Oesophageal carcinoma is inherently slow-growing, taking decades to become symptomatic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Oesophageal carcinoma is not characteristically slow-growing. Late presentation results from the absent serosa allowing silent circumferential spread, not from indolent tumour biology.

answers.text: Chronic acid reflux symptoms overshadow early tumour-related dysphagia, delaying investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While reflux may coexist, the primary reason for late presentation is the absent serosal layer, which permits circumferential tumour spread without an early physical barrier or symptoms.

overallFeedback.feedback: The oesophagus is the only major GI organ without a serosal layer. This allows carcinoma to spread circumferentially through the wall without early resistance, resulting in late presentation with dysphagia that progresses from solids to liquids.

Correct. The oesophagus uniquely lacks a serosa, allowing carcinoma to infiltrate circumferentially through the wall before causing luminal obstruction — explaining why patients present late with dysphagia progressing from solids to liquids.

interactions.label: An elderly woman presents with fatigue, iron-deficiency anaemia, and a positive

params.question: An elderly woman presents with fatigue, iron-deficiency anaemia, and a positive faecal occult blood test, but no change in bowel habit or visible rectal bleeding. Where is the colorectal carcinoma most likely located?

answers.text: Rectum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Rectal carcinoma typically presents with visible rectal bleeding, tenesmus, and altered bowel habit — not occult bleeding with isolated anaemia.

answers.text: Sigmoid colon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The sigmoid colon is part of the narrow left colon. Left-sided carcinoma tends to encircle the lumen as a napkin-ring stricture, causing early obstruction with pencil-thin stools and frank rectal bleeding.

answers.text: Ascending (right) colon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Right-sided colon cancer grows as a polypoid, fungating mass in the capacious right colon. The wide lumen accommodates the mass without obstruction, but slow, occult bleeding causes iron-deficiency anaemia — often the sole presenting finding.

answers.text: Descending (left) colon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Left-sided carcinoma encircles the narrower descending colon as a napkin-ring stricture. It typically causes early obstruction with altered bowel habit and frank rectal bleeding, not isolated anaemia.

overallFeedback.feedback: Right-sided colon cancer grows in the capacious right colon as a polypoid mass, causing slow occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia. Left-sided cancer encircles the narrower left colon as a napkin-ring stricture, causing early obstruction with altered bowel habit and frank rectal bleeding.

Excellent. The wide right colon accommodates a growing mass without obstruction, so right-sided cancer presents insidiously with occult bleeding and anaemia — a key anatomical principle explaining why these tumours are often detected late.
